video_title: Kimberly Gallant, Global Head of QIS Structuring, CIBC
gist: Kimberly Gallant (CIBC's global head of QIS structuring) walks through how quantitative investment strategies are built and vetted, covering the WTI/Brent vega asymmetry, the 2026 petroleum-driven commodity-curve drawdown, crowding diagnostics, and shifting client demand for de-dollarization and convex tail hedges amid a higher-rate regime and record-low equity correlation.

insights.claim: The modern QIS (quantitative investment strategies) industry emerged from the convergence of four distinct traditions in the 2010s: academic factor theory (Fama-French style research), CTA and pension-fund efforts to rethink risk models and asset allocation, post-GFC Volcker Rule-driven transfer of prop-desk IP into client-facing products, and the commodity index business.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: QIS strategies still carry the DNA of the tradition they descend from; investors diligencing a QIS product should ask which lineage (academic, CTA/pension, prop-desk, commodity) it comes from to judge the source of its edge.
insights.quote: what's fascinating about QIS is that it isn't just one origin story.

insights.claim: Well-designed QIS strategies should start from an economic hypothesis about who is on the other side of the trade and why, and only then be back-tested; strategies developed backtest-first tend to produce less favorable, overfit outcomes.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: When diligencing a quant/QIS manager, ask whether the economic thesis or the backtest came first — it is a fast way to flag data-mined, overfit strategies before allocating.
insights.quote: If back test comes first, you tend to find that outcomes are less favorable.

insights.claim: The QIS industry as a whole is described as structurally overindexed on backtested results — jokingly referred to as the 'backtesting Olympics' — which the head of CIBC's QIS structuring desk flags as a real weakness in how new strategies get developed and sold.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Investors should discount headline backtested Sharpe ratios shown by QIS desks industry-wide and demand independent economic rationale plus regime-dependency testing before allocating capital.
insights.quote: This whole industry is overindexed on back tests.

insights.claim: Insurance companies with guaranteed annuity products (effectively short a put to the policyholder) and banks managing regulatory capital are structural, capital-constrained buyers of downside equity puts, and will pay above fair value for them because holding the unhedged tail risk would cost more in regulatory or solvency terms — this is the structural source of the equity volatility carry premium.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: As long as insurers and banks retain these capital-driven mandates to buy tail protection, systematic short-volatility/carry strategies on S&P tails should retain a structural premium worth harvesting.
insights.quote: These market participants will pay above fair value for puts because the alternative holding the unhedged tail risk is ultimately going to cost them more in regulatory or solveny terms

insights.claim: The market-standard method for harvesting equity volatility risk premium has evolved from the VIX roll trade, to delta-hedged straddles/strangles, to daily-rolled variance swaps (to smooth gamma and monetize skew), and most recently to a daily strip of short-dated options replicating a '1/K^2' variance-swap payoff — a bounded structure clients now prefer over an unbounded variance swap.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Investors evaluating a VRP product should identify which 'vintage' of structure they are being offered — the modern options-replication approach caps downside risk in a way legacy unbounded variance swaps did not.

insights.claim: WTI and Brent crude are structurally different volatility markets: since the shale boom stretched North American producer balance sheets, WTI's dominant options flow has shifted from producers buying outright puts to producers running net short-vega three-way put-spread collars, while Brent sees net vega buying driven by macro funds, consumers, and non-North American producers.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: This structural WTI/Brent vega asymmetry supports relative-value volatility trades (e.g., selling Brent vol vs. buying WTI vol, or the reverse) as a way to isolate the risk premium rather than treating crude vol as one undifferentiated market.

themes.theme: Commodity Carry, the 2026 Petroleum Drawdown & Crowding Evidence

insights.claim: The classic diversified commodity time-spread carry strategy ('commodity curve') delivered Sharpe ratios of roughly 4-6 pre-2000 as a genuine alpha source, but has compressed to about 1.0 over the last two decades as more capital entered the space — still attractive given its low correlation to equity and bond risk premia, but no longer a true alpha source.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Sharpe-ratio compression over time is a measurable signature of factor maturation/crowding investors can track when judging whether a strategy's current expected return still justifies an allocation.

insights.claim: Earlier in 2026, the commodity curve (time-spread) strategy suffered the largest drawdown in its roughly two-decade trading history, driven entirely by the petroleum complex, with the magnitude of the move in time spreads far exceeding the outright price move — while the rest of the commodity complex showed no contagion.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: The absence of cross-complex contagion is itself a diagnostic signal that the 2026 drawdown was a legitimate, uncrowded risk-transfer event rather than a forced systemic unwind — an argument for holding the strategy through the loss rather than exiting.

insights.claim: Individual commodity time-spread markets cluster into related groups (e.g., gasoline, heating oil, gas oil, Brent and WTI move together) but the broader commodity complex is largely uncorrelated with itself — structurally less correlated than equity sectors are with each other — which is the core reason diversified commodity-curve books have historically been resilient to localized shocks.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: The diversification benefit of a multi-commodity carry book depends on these low cross-commodity correlations holding; a breakdown in that pattern (as seen in 2012) is an early warning sign of factor crowding.

insights.claim: In the summer 2012 North American drought, commodity time-spread losses genuinely spread across unrelated markets (natural gas, corn, soybeans all drew down together), a contagion event that coincided with some banks having sold 15x-levered structured notes linked to the commodity-curve complex with a knockout triggered at a 2% strategy loss — illustrating how leveraged, retail-distributed products can turn an ordinary carry drawdown into a forced, correlated unwind.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Leveraged structured-note issuance tied to a popular factor strategy is a leading indicator of crowding risk and a potential trigger for forced liquidation at the next tail event; investors should track how much leveraged product is outstanding on a factor before relying on its historical diversification.
insights.quote: some other banks had sold 15 times levered structured notes linked to the commodity curve pl complex with a knockout that was down uh if the market if the strategy was down 2%.

insights.claim: Crowding is hard to detect in real time because early-stage inflows into a popular strategy actually push its near-term returns higher (creating a false signal of persistent alpha), so crowding is usually only revealed when a tail event forces a leveraged, correlated unwind.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Rising short-term returns in a popular factor strategy should raise suspicion rather than comfort, since the outperformance may reflect crowding-driven inflows rather than durable edge.
insights.quote: it's hard to tell if a strategy is crowded in the beginning because yes, the premium's getting compressed, but the inflows actually are driving the value of that portfolio up.

insights.claim: The clearest diagnostic for crowding is unexplained correlation clustering during a drawdown — when strategy components move together without an underlying economic or fundamental linkage tying them to the same real-world event, that is a strong signal of crowded positioning rather than genuine risk transfer.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Risk managers should map each drawdown component back to a fundamental cause in real time; unexplained co-movement across otherwise unrelated positions is an actionable trigger to de-risk before a forced unwind accelerates.
insights.quote: If math and the theory don't align, it's usually time to take a deeper look.

themes.theme: Macro Regime Shift: Rates, Inflation & Stock-Bond Correlation

insights.claim: As of the interview, the 30-year Treasury yield is around 5.3% and crude oil is around $93/barrel, a sharp contrast to the prior decade's low-rate, low-volatility regime — a shift that materially complicates backtesting for strategies (especially inflation hedges) that were never tested through a genuine rising-rate, rising-inflation environment.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Allocators should discount backtest-derived performance for inflation-hedging and other regime-sensitive strategies that lack real historical data from a comparable rising-rate, high-inflation period like the current one.

insights.claim: The stock-bond correlation turns structurally positive once inflation runs above roughly 3%, which is the underlying economic driver of bonds' recent failure to hedge equity drawdowns and is fueling client demand for inflation-hedging and alternative diversification strategies.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: With inflation elevated, investors should not assume bonds will cushion equity drawdowns and should actively seek non-bond diversifiers (trend-following, tail hedges, QIS fixed-income replacement) instead.
insights.quote: we know that that correlation tends to run positive when inflation is above 3%.

insights.claim: With bonds no longer reliably hedging equities, unusually low single-stock correlation within equity indices has effectively been acting as a hidden 'free hedge' cushioning the market — and if that low-correlation regime ever breaks (i.e., stocks start moving together again) while stock-bond correlation stays positive, the resulting drawdown could be worse than markets currently expect, since neither traditional buffer would be available simultaneously.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: Monitor realized single-stock correlation alongside stock-bond correlation as a combined tail-risk indicator; a simultaneous spike in both would remove two current market buffers at once and could trigger an outsized equity selloff.
insights.quote: It feels a bit like there's been a bit of a free hedge that has been riding under the surface. Well, bonds haven't been doing their job to hedge equities.

themes.theme: Equity Dispersion & the AI Correlation Puzzle

insights.claim: Realized correlation among S&P 500 constituents is near an all-time low, which has driven the equity dispersion trade to unusually high profitability and popularity — and strikingly, even the 'Magnificent Seven' AI mega-caps are internally uncorrelated, with Microsoft's correlation to the other six Mag7 names running negative over the trailing month.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: The dispersion trade's profitability is directly tied to this correlation compression; watch for any snap-back higher in realized correlation as a signal that could hurt dispersion positions broadly.
insights.quote: I just looked at the correlation of Microsoft to the other six in the MAG seven and at least over the last month, it's negative.

insights.claim: Ultra-low realized stock correlation is observed not just in the AI-driven S&P 500 but broadly across global indices (Euro Stoxx, Nikkei, CAC, DAX) with far less AI concentration, raising the possibility that the phenomenon is partly self-reinforcing — i.e., the popularity of selling correlation via the dispersion trade may itself be suppressing realized correlation, rather than AI narratives alone explaining it.
insights.speaker: Dean Curnutt (host)
insights.so_what: If dispersion-trade flow is itself partly causing low correlation (a reflexive dynamic), the current low-correlation regime could be more fragile and prone to a sharp mean-reversion than a purely AI-driven explanation would imply.
insights.quote: This low correlation is everywhere in equity markets and I just don't know if it's a case where the product the the consumption of selling correlation is itself creating low correlation.

insights.claim: QIS clients are increasingly asking how to manage concentrated AI/mega-cap exposure risk from outsized allocations or recent IPO positions while still capturing further upside, a dynamic that is partly why spot-volatility correlation has turned positive during rallies (implied vol rising alongside gains) rather than following its historical negative relationship with the market.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: The breakdown of the classic negative spot-vol correlation means investors can no longer count on volatility spiking automatically on selloffs as a natural hedge; AI-driven concentration risk increasingly needs bespoke, purpose-built hedges.

themes.theme: Client Demand: De-Dollarization, Tail Hedging & Fixed-Income Replacement

insights.claim: Canadian and broader G10 pension and institutional investors are running structurally large, largely unhedged USD overlays — Gallant cites cases of investors effectively long roughly 50% US dollar exposure versus their home currency — built up over a multi-decade dollar bull run plus growing allocation to US-dominated private markets, and are now seeking QIS factor strategies to de-dollarize.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: A wave of de-dollarization hedging demand from G10 pension funds is a structural flow worth watching — it could act as a slow, persistent headwind for USD strength against G10 currencies as institutions unwind decades of unhedged dollar exposure.
insights.quote: they find themselves running long 50% US dollar overlay versus whatever the home currency is.

insights.claim: Despite elevated macro uncertainty and equity concentration risk, current QIS client demand skews toward tail-risk strategies with positive convexity and lower ongoing carry cost rather than classic long-volatility, carry-negative hedges — clients want asymmetric protection without paying heavy continuous premium.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: This demand pattern implies structural buying pressure for capital-efficient convex hedge structures (options ratios, trend-following, intraday momentum) over straightforward long-vol positions — relevant for anyone structuring or trading against this client flow.
insights.quote: we're not seeing as much demand for strategies where you pay away carry, which is a little bit counterintuitive given there's so much uncertainty bubbling under the surface.

insights.claim: Put-ratio (sell-one-buy-two) tail-hedge strategies performed well through the 2020 market shock but suffered compounding losses through the 'Liberation Day' tariff-driven shock, showing that a popular convex hedge structure's track record in one crisis does not guarantee performance in the next.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Investors relying on put-ratio tail hedges should stress-test them specifically against sharp, policy-driven shocks rather than assuming past crisis performance (e.g., 2020) will repeat in the next type of tail event.
insights.quote: Put ratios had been something that had been very popular. They performed very well through 2020 and then had compounded losses through liberation day.

insights.claim: Fixed-income beta replacement — QIS strategies built to replicate the traditional risk-buffering ('ballast') role bonds used to play in a 60/40 portfolio via positive-carry hedge structures — is a growing area of client demand as bonds have stopped reliably offsetting equity drawdowns.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: Watch for continued growth in synthetic/QIS 'bond replacement' products as a structural response to the broken stock-bond correlation — a potential growth product line for structuring desks and an allocation option for investors seeking ballast.

insights.claim: CIBC's QIS platform deliberately seeks out sophisticated institutional clients who will try to 'break' or stress-test a proposed strategy before launch, rather than clients who simply approve it, treating adversarial client feedback as core to the research and vetting process.
insights.speaker: Kimberly Gallant
insights.so_what: This is a useful due-diligence question for allocators: ask a QIS or structuring desk whether and how clients stress-tested a strategy pre-launch as part of manager selection.
insights.quote: we want to break the strategy before it goes live. And that's genuinely one of the most rewarding parts of the job.
